newsitem.title: USA: Wheat hits 10-month high, coffee also soars.
newsitem.headline: Wheat hits 10-month high, coffee also soars.

text.p: Wheat prices soared to 10-month highs on Friday as worries about potential poor crops in the United States and Europe gripped the market.

Coffee prices also soared on supply worries while copper firmed as workers in Chile struck at the world's largest copper exporter. Oil prices rose as cold weather persisted in the Northeast, the top heating oil market.
The Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 commodity futures ended 2.03 points higher at 247.34.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery closed 11-3/4 cents a bushel higher at $4.37 after hitting a high of $4.38, the highest level since May 28.
"There are all kinds of horror stories and they pulled some rain out of Europe. All of a sudden we've gone from bearish to bullish in a week," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.
The European Union on Thursday halted its weekly wheat export tenders to preserve supplies amid worries about a possible drought in France, the top European wheat grower.

But traders also cited persistent talk that last weekend's freeze in the U.S. Great Plains may have damaged up to 200 million bushels of wheat, with half of that in Kansas, the top U.S. wheat growing state.

"Those numbers for Kansas alone are not unrealistic," said Rollie Sears, a Kansas State University wheat breeder, who toured the damaged areas this week. "The damage in the southern third of the state is worse than I thought."
Fears that flooding in the Red River Valley of North Dakota, a key growing area for spring wheat and sugar beets, could delay or cut plantings also supported futures prices.
"It's cold and wet, nothing is going on. We are going to have late planting right across the whole state," said Lance Gaebe of the North Dakota Grain Growers Association.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee prices rose for the third day in a row as worry about tight stocks resumed its hold on traders.
Coffee for May delivery closed up 6.75 cents at 216.55 cents a pound.
A monthly report earlier this week from the Green Coffee Association of New York estimated that warehouse stocks of coffee in the United States were much smaller than expected at the end of March.

That was followed by news of a port strike in Brazil, the top coffee exporter, and a planned truckers' strike in Ciolombia, the number two exporter. Meanwhile, roasters are scrambling to secure coffee supplies.
Coffee in warehouses certified for delivery at the exchange fell 16,729 bags to 63,349 bags in the two days ending on Thursday.

"CSCE warehouse coffee stocks fell sharply, and you have strikes or potential strikes going on in Brazil and Colombia, so it's hard to imagine how much more bullish you can get," Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka said.
Coffee futures rose to a 2-1/2 year high of 227.50 cents in the first week of March, more than doubling since November.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices rose in largely technical trade but with heating oil supported by lingering cold weather in the northeastern United States.
Crude oil for May delivery ended 49 cents higher at $19.91 a barrel. May heating oil ended 0.68 cent higher at 54.68 cents a gallon and May gasoline 0.79 cent higher at 61.49 cents a gallon.

The National Weather Service forecast issued on Friday for the period from April 24 to 28 said below normal temperatures were expected for the Northeast, Midwest and Plains states, extending the chill of winter and heating needs.
Traders said buying in crude oil was also tied to the expiration of the May futures contract on Tuesday.

Copper prices closed higher on news that 120 workers belonging to a small union at Chile's huge Escondida copper mine went on strike. Other members of the union were expected to join their striking colleagues, labor leaders said.
About 2,000 miners work at the facility, but the company said the action would have no immediate effect on operations.
Copper for May delivery on the COMEX in New York closed at 106.80 cents a pound, up 1.25 cents.
